name: AD8656ARMZ-REEL
title: AD8655/AD8656: low-noise precision CMOS rail-to-rail op amps, single and dual, 28 MHz, 2.7 V to 5.5 V
summary: A single (AD8655) and dual (AD8656) CMOS operational amplifier whose input and output both swing to the rails, 2.7 nV/√Hz voltage noise at 10 kHz and an offset of 250 µV max across the whole common-mode range, trimmed after packaging. Gain-bandwidth is 28 MHz at 5 V and the output delivers ±220 mA; it runs from 2.7 V to 5.5 V over −40°C to +125°C and is unity-gain stable. Packages are 8-lead MSOP and SOIC; automotive-qualified W models exist in MSOP. AD8656ARMZ-REEL is the dual in MSOP on a reel.

circuits.title: Snubber for a heavy capacitive load
circuits.description: A unity-gain follower driving 500 pF. The output feeds the load capacitor C2 and, beside it, a series 200 Ω resistor and 500 pF capacitor (R1, C1) to ground. That RC pair damps the ringing a large load capacitance causes and cuts the overshoot by over 30 %, without costing output swing; the bandwidth lost to the heavy load stays lost. The test signal is a 200 mV step into +IN.
notes: Measured with VS = ±2.5 V, AV = 1, RS = 200 Ω, CS = 500 pF, CL = 500 pF.

circuits.title: THD + N test circuit
circuits.description: The amplifier runs as a voltage follower from ±2.5 V supplies. A signal generator drives +IN against ground, the output is tied straight back to -IN, and RL loads the output to ground; distortion is measured at VOUT.

parts.note: 1 kΩ or 10 kΩ in the THD + N sweeps

circuits.title: Channel separation test circuit
circuits.description: Amplifier A is a follower driven with 50 mV p-p; its output connects only to its own inverting input. Amplifier B has +IN B grounded, R1 (10 kΩ) from OUT B to -IN B and R2 (100 Ω) from -IN B to ground; its output is VOUT. Supplies are ±2.5 V.

operation.text: Voltage-feedback CMOS amplifiers whose inputs and outputs both swing rail to rail, specified at 2.7 V and 5.0 V supplies (the operating range is 2.7 V to 5.5 V). Offset is trimmed after packaging (DigiTrim), so offset caused by assembly stress is trimmed out too; the pinouts are standard op amp pinouts. The input stage common-mode range reaches both supply rails. Open-loop gain into 10 kΩ is 110 dB typical. Both parts are unity-gain stable.
The output does not reverse phase for any input common-mode voltage within the supplies.
At 10 kHz and 2 V p-p, THD + N measures −103 dB; voltage noise is 2.7 nV/√Hz and input bias current under a picoamp.
With a 1 kΩ load, THD is well below 0.0007 %. It varies with the circuit configuration, the applied voltage and the layout.

Internal protection tolerates input voltages beyond the supplies, but neither input should go more than 0.3 V past a rail. Where larger inputs can occur, put a resistor in series with the input and keep the input current under 5 mA. Because bias current is so small, the series resistor can be large; its thermal noise adds to the output noise. A 10 kΩ resistor contributes under 12.6 nV/√Hz and under 10 nV of error at room temperature.

In a circuit with resistive feedback, the total capacitance at an input (source, stray or the amplifier's own) puts a break in the noise gain, and a capacitor in parallel with the gain resistor is needed for stability. The noise gain rises with frequency and peaks at the high end when the feedback capacitor sets a critically damped second-order response. A few picofarads at an input lower its impedance at high frequency, raising the gain and causing peaking or oscillation. With the output fed straight back to the input, a capacitive load above 200 pF needs extra input damping.

The amplifier stays free of oscillation with loads as large as 500 pF, but rings heavily for inputs above 100 kHz, worst as a non-inverting unity-gain buffer. For such loads external compensation is strongly advised: an RC snubber (200 Ω in series with 500 pF, from the output to ground) keeps the output swing, makes the circuit stable at all gains, cuts overshoot by over 30 % and removes the ringing. It does not win back the bandwidth lost to the load.

Bypass each supply with a 0.1 µF ceramic chip capacitor (X7R or NPO) as close to the package as possible, in parallel with 4.7 µF tantalum; the tantalum matters less at high frequency, and usually a single one where the supply enters the board is enough.

On a densely packed board a ground plane keeps parasitic inductance low. Keep leads of the high-frequency bypass capacitors short (surface-mount parts); any inductance in the ground trace of a bypass capacitor undoes it. Return the load to ground at the same spot as the bypass capacitors, since load current comes from the supplies. Return path length matters less for the larger, low-frequency capacitors.

Board contamination, layout and the insulator itself can leak far more current than the input bias current. Surround the inputs and their leads with a guard ring driven from a low impedance at the input potential, on all sides and on the layers above and below in a multilayer board. Charge absorption in the insulator also leaks: keep the insulator between guard ring and input leads thin, and where needed use PTFE, ceramic or another low-absorption material.

The W models (AD8655WARMZ-RL, AD8656WARMZ-REEL) are built under controlled manufacturing for automotive quality and reliability requirements and are the only grades for automotive use; their specifications can be different from those of the commercial grades.
